source.title: Acceleration of Grokking in Learning Arithmetic Operations via Kolmogorov-Arnold Representation
source.authors: Yeachan Park; Minseok Kim; Yeoneung Kim

page_placements.theme: Transfer and reuse of grokked components

record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking on small algorithmic arithmetic tasks using reported steps to grokking and final accuracy, but studies acceleration methods rather than directly reproducing the original training recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper reports grokking outcomes for arithmetic-operation training and compares augmentation and weight-transfer conditions. PCA embedding visualizations and algebraic representation arguments do not measure gradual circuit formation. Claims about other data types, low-norm mechanisms, same algorithms across runs, and optimizer or numerical artifacts are not tested.
record.test_reason: The paper treats grokking as a target to speed up. It reports steps until test accuracy exceeds 99% for its own augmentation and weight-transfer methods against a vanilla baseline. No training-accuracy curves are given, so it cannot show test accuracy rising long after training accuracy saturates, or from chance. The PCA circle plots illustrate the embedding but do not track circuit formation (V2) or compare algorithms across runs (V6). No other version is examined.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that commutative augmentation and weight transfer accelerate grokking on modular arithmetic, composition and equation-system tasks. They justify the transfer methods with Kolmogorov-Arnold representation arguments. They also claim embedding transfer allows learning with a limited set of tokens, which they say shows the model learns the rules rather than memorizing.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a transformer on algorithmically generated arithmetic tasks over Zp with p = 97, but focuses on commutative augmentation and decoder-block or embedding transfer. The reported grokking criterion is test accuracy exceeding 99% within 105 steps.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with task, training sample count, augmentation or transfer condition, and token count. Augmentation sometimes fails to produce grokking or takes more steps than baseline; transfer is reported to enable grokking in several otherwise non-grokked conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Algebra-motivated interventions change the time to 99% test accuracy on modular arithmetic tasks. Decoder-block or embedding transfer cuts steps by about 5–20x and enables grokking where baselines fail. Commutative augmentation helps inconsistently.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking delay on algorithmic tasks can be shortened by transferring structurally shared components (embedding or decoder block) or by symmetry augmentation.

record.problems: No training-accuracy trajectories are reported, so the paper does not directly establish perfect training accuracy before the test-accuracy rise. It defines grokking as test accuracy exceeding 99% within 105 steps, but some tables mark results Grokked alongside numeric final accuracies below 99% or provide no numeric final accuracy. The number of runs is not stated in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted baseline comparator rows marked Grokked where the corresponding main intervention rows are retained: Table 1 successful baselines for addition, multiplication, and the other listed operations; Table 2 successful baselines apart from the non-grokked (x1 + x2)^3 comparator; Table 3 successful baselines for x1 + x2 + x3 at N = 100000 and 300000, x1 × x2 × x3 at N = 300000; Table 4 multiplication baselines. These were left out to keep within 60 rows and prioritize non-grokked outcomes and conditions that change the result.

untested.parts: Training-accuracy saturation before the test-accuracy rise, and a rise from chance. Baseline grokking steps across N exist, but only as time to 99% test accuracy.
All. The PCA embedding circles are a single snapshot, with no progress measures.
All. Weight decay is fixed at 0.1 and never varied.
All. There is no cross-run algorithm comparison.

missing.what: Baseline grokking steps across training-set sizes. For x1^3+x2^3+x1+x2: 6304, 12929, 48769 steps at N=5000/4000/3000. For x1^2+x2^2+x1+x2: 584, 3374, then non-grokked at N=6000/5000/4000. For x1+x2 the trend is non-monotonic: 27167 at N=5000, 15359 at N=4000. These bear on V1's dataset-size trend, but only as time to 99% test accuracy; rows_left_out drops several of them.

record.verdict_notes: Grokking here is defined as test accuracy over 99% within 10^5 steps. No training curves are shown, so the delay after overfitting is never measured; the paper only asserts it. The number of runs is not stated. Several '± 0' entries suggest a single run or degenerate variance. Uses AdamW with weight decay 0.1 at p=97, close to the Power et al. recipe.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report training-accuracy trajectories or establish that training accuracy saturated while test accuracy remained at chance. The reported dataset-size results do not consistently establish that smaller training sets require more optimization.
Gradual formation and removal of circuits, and whether progress measures anticipate the test-accuracy jump.
Non-algorithmic data and initialization-scale or weight-norm changes.
LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
Whether low-norm bias causes efficient circuits, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking.
Whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
Adaptive-optimizer instabilities and floating-point or softmax artifacts.

relation.reason: Treats grokking as a phenomenon to accelerate and evaluates its own methods without measuring the defining trajectories or mechanisms in the claim versions.

tranche.reason: Reports performance of augmentation and transfer methods using steps to a test-accuracy threshold; it does not establish the training-saturation-to-generalization delay or test another claim version.

source_check.notes: The listed rows are own-method comparisons, not direct tests of a claim version. Threshold crossing alone does not establish delayed generalization after training accuracy saturates.

statements.correction: Section 5.1.2: criterion is test accuracy exceeding 99% within 100000 steps. Table 2: multiplication, N=5000, baseline 20367±13414 steps versus decoder transfer 3939±3421; x1^2+x2^2+x1+x2, N=5000, baseline 755±293 versus transfer 359±50. Table 3: three-operand addition, N=10000, baseline non-grokked with final accuracy 32.17±11.01 versus embedding transfer 29491±22414 steps, grokked.
statements.problem: Transfer accelerates threshold crossing and succeeds in some settings where baselines fail, but the stated 5–20× range omits smaller reported speedups and is not explicitly reported in the text.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported grokked conditions across arithmetic operations, compositions, equation-solving tasks, and limited-token tasks
reader_labels.reason: The tables report grokking after training in these algorithmic settings, although they do not show the training-accuracy plateau or chance-level test phase; see T1-a1–T1-a2, T1-a4–T1-a5, T1-a7–T1-a13, T2-d1–T2-d7, T3-e1–T3-e8, T4-e1–T4-e4, T5-e1–T5-e2.
